ADA compliance deadline looms, Cole County officials' opinions split on plans | Jefferson City News Tribune

# ADA compliance deadline looms, Cole County officials' opinions split on plans

 March 29, 2026 by Matthew McFarland 

Julie Smith/News Tribune File Photo: Cole County Eastern District Commissioner Jeff Hoelscher, foreground, Presiding Commissioner Sam Bushman and Western District Commissioner Harry Otto are shown during a Jan. 13, 2026, Cole County Commission meeting.

Cole County has a month to make all of its digital resources compliant with the American with Disabilities Act (ADA) or face the risk of potential lawsuits and federal penalties.

The county expects to meet that deadline one way or another, Western District County Commissioner Harry Otto said Friday, though what Cole County's website will look like after the remediation remains to be seen.

Local governments with more than 50,000 residents are required to update their online resources to comply with ADA standards by a U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) deadline of April 24. Compliance with the standards includes accessibility options like screen readers for government documents, descriptive text for photos and documents that can be navigated using only a keyboard.

Federal penalties are not likely to be handed out immediately after the deadline if local governments are found to be acting in good faith, according to previous reporting. Still, federal penalties could be substantial, with DOJ fines reaching up to $115,000, according to a 2025 tip sheet published by the State of Delaware's Government Information Center.

The county will also be eager to avoid lawsuits from trigger-happy attorneys suing them over ADA compliance, Otto said. Last year, the county ended a decade-long lawsuit against the prosecuting attorney's office that cost the county more $189,000 in taxpayer money, according to previous reporting.

The DOJ operates under a similar reporting system to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). If a citizen reports a breach of ADA guidelines and a fine is issued, the reporter is entitled to retain some of the fine, according to Dave Bandré, a local attorney familiar with the ADA compliance process through his role as the city counsel of Wardsville and Taos.

The strain

ADA compliance standards apply not just to applications and agendas, but to bids, vendor contracts and any document that is not considered officially archived.

For some county departments, like Cole County Public Works and the Cole County Collector's Office, that means truckloads of work to backlog years of documentation.

"We have historical records on the past 10 years of bids ... it's all online, they (contractors and interested parties) can just search it," Eric Landwehr, Cole County Public Works director, said on Wednesday. "It's a benefit to anybody bidding on our projects or anyone wanting to look at them. So now that information is out there, and we have to convert it all. It's just not possible."

For departments like Landwehr's, the fast-approaching compliance deadline means they'll be put in a catch-22 -- either struggle through ADA compliance standards or delete the document entirely, Landwehr said.

"We're having to adhere to this federal mandate, and the way to do it is just remove information," Landwehr said. "I don't think that's right. It's counterproductive."

Otto laid out a less removal-heavy plan on Friday. The county recently secured software that will allow it to see which online resources are being used most, according to previous reporting. Using that data, Otto said the county plans to make the most-used resources compliant by the deadline while deleting less-used or harder to change documents and uploading them again later once they meet ADA standards.

Whether the resources go back online or not, changing them to adhere to ADA standards will take a lot of manpower. County Collector Larry Vincent, who gave a fiery account of his opinion to the commission at its Tuesday meeting, county departments shouldn't have to bear the brunt of the workload of ADA compliance.

"It's a challenge, you know? None of my people are IT people. I'm more interested in them taking care of taxpayers and those functions that we're statutorily required to do than taking on new projects that are hit and miss because we're not familiar with it," Vincent said Wednesday. "That's why I'd like the commission to take a position on this rather than expecting each elected official to have somebody in their office take care of it."

The timeline

Several county officials expressed concern at the last-minute nature of the push for ADA compliance. The issue had not been discussed in a formal public meeting until March 3, when Cole County Geographical Information Systems manager Melissa Johnson said the amount of things to learn was "mind-boggling."

Cole County is big enough to face the more accelerated federal timeline (a deadline that Jefferson City will not face until April 2027), but not large enough to have the resources of the state's most populous municipalities and counties.

Brian Ridenhour, Cole County Information Systems director, heads a team of four people; his team, along with Johnson, are leading the county's compliance efforts. Neither Ridenhour nor Johnson responded to multiple requests for an interview.

Greene County, which faces the same deadline as Cole, boasts an information systems staff of 32 people, according to salary information obtained through a Sunshine Law request.

"I've asked the commission to put out an RFP (request for proposal) just to get a sense of what it would cost to contract with somebody to bring all our stuff up to date," Vincent said. "I think that would make it more manageable for each office to take care of it going forward."

The commission on Tuesday approved a $7,000 contract with Continual Engine, a software firm promising "AI-powered accessibility solutions," according to its website. The artificial intelligence will be used as a grading tool and compliance checker as documents are made ADA compliant, Otto said.

Otto didn't rule out the possibility of the commission spending more funds to aid in document remediation, but said he didn't think the timeline was an issue.

Bandré said the deadline has been a long time coming. The DOJ set its deadline in 2024 when it passed a modernized version of its website accessiblity guidelines.

"Not representing (Cole County), it's tough for me to speak to them ... but I can tell you the first publication that basically required municipalities and state and local governments to comply with ADA is back from 1988," Bandré said Thursday. "The feds have been talking about this stuff for a long time."

Some departments got off easy, though, as not every department is scrambling to meet the deadline. The Cole County Sheriff's and Assessor's offices reported a breezy compliance process.

"I'd say the only real difficulty is trying to make sure that everything is squared away the first time instead having to go back," commercial appraiser Noah Lara said Wednesday while discussing user interface improvements, increased contrast text for easier reading and more-boiled-down language coming to the assessor's webpage.

"We're trying to focus on any documents that get a higher amount of traffic than submissions, making sure those are fixed first, and kind of working backwards from there," Lara said.

The News Tribune attempted to get statements and/or interviews on the ADA compliance process from every county department. The offices of the treasurer, prosecuting attorney, circuit clerk, clerk, and recorder of deeds did not respond to emails requesting interviews. The Cole County Health and Information Systems departments also did not respond.
